game_title: Commanders of the Cosmos: Space Mission Design Adventure

questions.story: Welcome to Mission Control, Commander! Your engineering team is ready to design a brand-new robotic space mission. Every choice you make will change your spacecraft's weight, power, budget, and discoveries.
questions.question: Which destination will your mission explore?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Explore the Moon, Earth's closest neighbor.
answers.consequence_summary: A 3-day trip saves mission budget and keeps radio signals strong, while offering solid lunar science.
answers.learning_point: The Moon is about 384,400 km away, making travel faster, cheaper, and easier for radio communication than deep space.

answers.text: Explore Mars, the distant Red Planet.
answers.consequence_summary: A multi-month deep-space journey costs more budget and weakens radio signals, but unlocks huge scientific rewards.
answers.learning_point: Mars is millions of kilometers away, requiring more fuel, stronger radios, and higher budgets for big discoveries.

questions.story: Your lunar mission is approved! Now your science team needs a clear primary goal so engineers know what kind of spacecraft to build.
questions.question: What is your main scientific objective on the Moon?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Map sunlit lunar plains to study surface rocks and minerals.
answers.consequence_summary: Sunlit regions make solar power easy and keep costs low.
answers.learning_point: Sunlit areas on the Moon receive steady sunlight for two weeks at a time, ideal for solar-powered spacecraft.

answers.text: Search dark polar craters for frozen water ice.
answers.consequence_summary: Finding water ice is a major discovery, but permanently shadowed craters are freezing cold and lack sunlight.
answers.learning_point: Deep craters near the Moon's poles never see sunlight, trapping ancient water ice in extreme cold.

questions.story: Your Mars mission team gathers around the planetary map. Mars has a thin atmosphere and ancient dry riverbeds.
questions.question: What is your primary scientific goal at Mars?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Study the Martian atmosphere and track global dust storms.
answers.consequence_summary: An atmospheric orbiter avoids risky landing gear, saving mass and budget.
answers.learning_point: Studying a planet from orbit avoids the weight and risk of landing systems while watching weather across the whole globe.

answers.text: Investigate Mars's rocky crust and ancient water history.
answers.consequence_summary: Investigating rocks and subsurface layers requires heavier instruments and more power, but yields top-tier geology data.
answers.learning_point: Mars's rocks and underground layers hold chemical clues about whether ancient Mars once had lakes and rivers.

questions.story: To map the sunlit lunar surface, engineers need to build the spacecraft's main body—called the spacecraft bus—and its power system.
questions.question: Which spacecraft configuration will you build?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: A lightweight solar-panel bus with a standard small battery.
answers.consequence_summary: Keeps mass and cost low, though power drops whenever the spacecraft passes behind the Moon.
answers.learning_point: Lightweight spacecraft cost less to launch, but smaller batteries limit how much work they can do in the dark.

answers.text: A larger bus with dual high-capacity rechargeable batteries.
answers.consequence_summary: Adds weight and cost, but gives your mission plenty of stored energy for night operations.
answers.learning_point: Batteries store solar energy so a spacecraft can keep operating during lunar eclipses or night passes.

questions.story: Exploring dark polar craters on the Moon means temperatures can plunge below -200 degrees Celsius, where electronics can freeze.
questions.question: How will you protect your crater-hunting spacecraft?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Add gold multi-layer thermal blankets and electric heaters.
answers.consequence_summary: Heaters use electrical power and add moderate mass, but keep sensitive instruments alive.
answers.learning_point: Thermal insulation and heaters prevent spacecraft computers and batteries from freezing in shadowy space environments.

answers.text: Install a heavy-duty battery pack to power quick crater dives.
answers.consequence_summary: Boosts available power significantly, though the heavy batteries increase total spacecraft mass.
answers.learning_point: High-capacity batteries add significant mass, creating a classic engineering trade-off between energy and weight.

questions.story: At Mars, sunlight is less than half as bright as it is at Earth! Your atmospheric orbiter needs a smart design to gather enough energy.
questions.question: How will you configure your Mars orbiter?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Equip wide, high-efficiency solar wings.
answers.consequence_summary: Wide solar panels generate strong power at Mars without carrying heavy braking fuel.
answers.learning_point: Because Mars is farther from the Sun than Earth, solar-powered spacecraft need larger solar wings to capture enough light.

answers.text: Build a streamlined aerobraking frame to skim Mars's upper air.
answers.consequence_summary: Using atmospheric drag saves rocket fuel mass and budget, but requires careful heat protection.
answers.learning_point: Aerobraking uses friction from a planet's upper atmosphere to slow a spacecraft down, saving heavy fuel.

questions.story: Your science team wants to uncover how water once shaped Mars. You can either drive across the surface or scan deep underground from orbit.
questions.question: Which mission architecture will you choose?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Build a six-wheeled surface rover with a robotic arm.
answers.consequence_summary: Rovers deliver extraordinary hands-on science, but add major mass and budget cost.
answers.learning_point: Planetary rovers require heat shields, parachutes, and wheels, making them heavier and costlier than orbiters.

answers.text: Build a dedicated geological survey orbiter.
answers.consequence_summary: An orbiter is lighter, cheaper, and communicates easily with Earth while mapping large regions.
answers.learning_point: Orbiters can map an entire planet's geology over several years without the risk of landing.

questions.story: Your lightweight lunar spacecraft is ready for its science payload. Every instrument adds mass and draws power from your solar panels.
questions.question: Which primary scientific instrument will you install?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: A lightweight 3D stereo mapping camera.
answers.consequence_summary: Uses minimal power and mass while capturing detailed elevation maps of lunar craters.
answers.learning_point: Stereo cameras take two slightly offset pictures to build 3D maps of mountains and craters.

answers.text: A high-power laser mineral spectrometer.
answers.consequence_summary: Reveals exact rock chemistry for huge science points, but drains power and budget.
answers.learning_point: Spectrometers analyze reflected light to identify what chemical elements are inside lunar rocks.

questions.story: With dual batteries onboard, your spacecraft has extra energy reserves! You can use that power for mobility or wide-area mapping.
questions.question: How will you put your extra battery capacity to work?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Add a small lunar hopper module to visit multiple sites.
answers.consequence_summary: Hopping between sites boosts science, though propellant tanks add extra weight.
answers.learning_point: Because the Moon has only one-sixth of Earth's gravity, small thrusters let a spacecraft hop from crater to crater.

answers.text: Carry dual wide-angle and thermal mapping cameras in orbit.
answers.consequence_summary: Balanced weight and power while collecting continuous temperature and mineral maps.
answers.learning_point: Thermal cameras measure heat glowing off the lunar surface, showing where solid rock or fine dust lies.

questions.story: Your thermal blankets keep your spacecraft warm near the lunar poles. Now you need an instrument to confirm whether water ice is hidden in the dark soil.
questions.question: Which ice-hunting instrument will you choose?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: A neutron spectrometer that detects hydrogen from orbit.
answers.consequence_summary: Light and efficient—spots buried water molecules without touching the freezing surface.
answers.learning_point: Neutron spectrometers detect hydrogen atoms just beneath the lunar soil, a strong sign of hidden water ice.

answers.text: A heavy surface drill and soil-heating oven.
answers.consequence_summary: Directly tests real ice samples for massive science, but makes your spacecraft very heavy.
answers.learning_point: Drilling into frozen lunar soil requires heavy motors and extra power, greatly increasing total spacecraft mass.

questions.story: Inside permanently shadowed craters, normal cameras see only pitch blackness. You need an active instrument that creates its own beam.
questions.question: Which active sensor will you mount on your spacecraft?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: A laser altimeter that bounces light pulses into dark craters.
answers.consequence_summary: Maps crater floors and bright icy patches while keeping mass manageable.
answers.learning_point: Laser altimeters fire pulses of laser light to measure topography and spot bright ice patches in total darkness.

answers.text: A deep-penetrating ice radar sounder.
answers.consequence_summary: Sees thick ice layers underground, though it generates huge data files that need strong communications.
answers.learning_point: Radar sounders send radio waves beneath the surface to measure how thick buried ice sheets are.

questions.story: Your wide-winged Mars orbiter has plenty of solar power. Your atmospheric scientists have proposed two specialized instruments.
questions.question: Which atmospheric instrument will you fly?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: A neutral gas mass spectrometer to measure escaping air.
answers.consequence_summary: Light and low-power—helps explain how Mars lost its thick ancient atmosphere.
answers.learning_point: Mass spectrometers weigh individual gas molecules to see how solar wind strips away Mars's upper atmosphere.

answers.text: A high-power atmospheric dust and cloud lidar.
answers.consequence_summary: Tracks 3D dust storms in crisp detail, though the instrument adds substantial mass.
answers.learning_point: Lidar uses laser pulses to measure dust clouds and wind layers at different altitudes in the Martian sky.

questions.story: Aerobraking lets your orbiter dip into Mars's upper atmosphere to slow down without burning rocket fuel—but atmospheric friction creates intense heat!
questions.question: What thermal protection will you install for aerobraking?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Install tested ceramic-composite heat tiles on the leading edge.
answers.consequence_summary: Adds a little mass and budget, but safely absorbs friction heat during atmospheric passes.
answers.learning_point: Heat-resistant tiles protect spacecraft structures when friction with atmospheric gas molecules heats the hull.

answers.text: Skip extra heat shielding and use thin aluminum foil to save weight.
answers.consequence_summary: Saving weight without thermal protection causes critical overheating during atmospheric entry.
answers.learning_point: Cutting safety hardware below engineering limits can cause mission loss when extreme space heat strikes.

questions.story: Your Mars rover is taking shape! Unlike orbiters, a surface rover must survive freezing Martian nights and dusty skies.
questions.question: How will you power your Mars rover?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Use a radioisotope power system (MMRTG) for steady day-and-night energy.
answers.consequence_summary: Expensive and heavier, but provides reliable electricity and warmth through dust storms and winter nights.
answers.learning_point: Radioisotope power systems turn heat from natural radioactive decay into electricity, working even in dark dust storms.

answers.text: Use fold-out solar panels to save budget.
answers.consequence_summary: Saves budget and weight, though dust buildup on panels can reduce power over time.
answers.learning_point: Solar-powered Mars rovers are lighter and cheaper, but Martian dust can coat their solar panels and limit power.

questions.story: Your Mars geological orbiter is ready for its primary sensor. Your team wants to find where ancient water flowed.
questions.question: Which geological instrument will you choose?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: A subsurface ground-penetrating radar to search for buried ice.
answers.consequence_summary: Finds hidden underground water ice, creating large datasets to transmit back to Earth.
answers.learning_point: Subsurface radar sends radio pulses through Mars's crust to detect buried ice layers and ancient channels.

answers.text: A hyperspectral mineral imager to spot ancient clay deposits.
answers.consequence_summary: Identifies water-formed minerals across the surface with moderate power needs.
answers.learning_point: Hyperspectral imagers split reflected sunlight into hundreds of colors to spot clay minerals that only form in water.

questions.story: Your 3D stereo camera is bolted onto your lunar spacecraft. Now you must choose the orbit path around the Moon.
questions.question: Which lunar orbit will you select?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: A low 50 km polar mapping orbit for ultra-sharp photos.
answers.consequence_summary: Gives crystal-clear close-up images, though the spacecraft passes into the Moon's shadow every two hours.
answers.learning_point: Low polar orbits fly close to the entire Moon over time, giving sharp images while passing frequently through shadow.

answers.text: A higher elliptical orbit that stays in sunlight longer.
answers.consequence_summary: Keeps solar panels charged and radios linked to Earth for a reliable, steady mission.
answers.learning_point: Higher elliptical orbits spend more time in sunlight and in view of Earth antennas, making operations smoother.

questions.story: Your laser mineral spectrometer collects rich chemical data, but sending large files back to Earth takes strong radio equipment.
questions.question: Which communication system will you install?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Keep a small omni-directional antenna to save budget and mass.
answers.consequence_summary: Saves money, but slow data rates mean only part of your mineral map reaches Earth before mission end.
answers.learning_point: Small antennas broadcast weakly in all directions, limiting how much science data can be sent back to Earth.

answers.text: Install a steerable high-gain dish antenna.
answers.consequence_summary: Focuses radio signals directly toward Earth, downloading 100% of your mineral discoveries!
answers.learning_point: High-gain dish antennas focus radio waves into a narrow beam aimed at Earth, dramatically increasing data download speed.

questions.story: Your lunar hopper has landed! After studying its first crater, your team spots an intriguing ridge 2 kilometers away.
questions.question: How will you balance fuel and instruments for the hop?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Prioritize reserve thruster propellant and execute a short, controlled hop.
answers.consequence_summary: Safe fuel margins let you explore two craters and return valuable comparison data!
answers.learning_point: Keeping reserve propellant ensures a spacecraft can safely complete maneuvers without running out of fuel.

answers.text: Attempt a long-range leap across rugged terrain with minimal fuel margin.
answers.consequence_summary: Thrusters run dry mid-maneuver, leaving the hopper tilted in a shadowed gully unable to point its antenna.
answers.learning_point: Propellant is a strict, non-renewable resource in space—pushing beyond fuel margins risks losing the spacecraft.

questions.story: Your dual thermal and wide-angle cameras are ready in lunar orbit. Flight controllers ask you to set your mapping altitude.
questions.question: Which orbital altitude will you choose?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Fly at 50 km altitude for high-resolution thermal maps.
answers.consequence_summary: Your dual batteries easily power through short eclipses, delivering razor-sharp maps of the entire Moon!
answers.learning_point: Combining low-altitude orbits with strong battery reserves lets a spacecraft capture high-detail maps safely.

answers.text: Fly at 200 km altitude for wide regional coverage and gentle fuel use.
answers.consequence_summary: Uses very little station-keeping fuel and completes a smooth, efficient lunar survey.
answers.learning_point: Higher lunar orbits require less fuel to stay stable because uneven lunar gravity pulls less strongly farther out.

questions.story: Your neutron spectrometer found strong hydrogen signals inside a deep crater near the Moon's south pole! However, Earth sits very low on the horizon from the pole.
questions.question: How will you send your discovery data back to Earth?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Wait for brief direct line-of-sight windows with Earth.
answers.consequence_summary: Terrain blocks signals part of the time, so only summary data reaches Earth.
answers.learning_point: Radio waves travel in straight lines—crater rims and horizons can block direct communication with Earth.

answers.text: Beam data through a lunar relay satellite overhead.
answers.consequence_summary: The relay satellite bounces your signal cleanly around the Moon's edge, sending every byte home!
answers.learning_point: Relay satellites act like space mirrors for radio signals, connecting polar craters and the far side of the Moon to Earth.

questions.story: Launchpad check! Your ice-drilling lander is packed with heavy drills, heaters, and ovens—pushing your spacecraft mass into the heavy range.
questions.question: Which launch vehicle will you book for liftoff?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Book a budget-friendly medium-lift rocket.
answers.consequence_summary: Your heavy drilling lander exceeds the medium rocket's payload limit, grounding the mission before launch!
answers.learning_point: Every rocket has a maximum payload mass limit. If a spacecraft is too heavy, the rocket cannot reach escape velocity.

answers.text: Book a heavy-lift rocket matched to your lander's mass.
answers.consequence_summary: The heavy rocket lifts your drill safely to the Moon, confirming subsurface water ice!
answers.learning_point: Heavy-lift launch vehicles cost more budget, but they are essential for sending heavy landers and drills beyond Earth.

questions.story: Your laser altimeter spacecraft has a moderate mass and high-capacity batteries. Now it needs a ride to space!
questions.question: Which launch option will you choose?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Share a rocket ride with another mission to split launch costs.
answers.consequence_summary: Saves major budget and reaches lunar orbit smoothly on a shared trajectory.
answers.learning_point: Rideshare launches let smaller spacecraft share a rocket with larger payloads, saving millions in mission budget.

answers.text: Book a dedicated medium rocket for a direct polar trajectory.
answers.consequence_summary: Costs more budget, but places your spacecraft directly over the lunar poles for crisp ice-crater maps!
answers.learning_point: A dedicated launch lets engineers pick the exact launch window and orbit best suited for their science goal.

questions.story: Your deep-penetrating radar sounder has mapped thick layers of ice beneath the Moon's poles, generating gigabytes of radar echoes.
questions.question: How will you handle this massive flood of scientific data?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Use a high-frequency Ka-band radio transmitter.
answers.consequence_summary: High-frequency Ka-band beams down ultra-detailed radar maps of buried lunar ice!
answers.learning_point: Higher radio frequencies like Ka-band can carry far more scientific data per second than older S-band radios.

answers.text: Use onboard software compression to shrink files before sending.
answers.consequence_summary: Saves power and hardware weight while sending clean summary maps to Earth.
answers.learning_point: Onboard data compression reduces file sizes so spacecraft can transmit discoveries faster using less radio power.

questions.story: Your Mars atmospheric orbiter arrives at the Red Planet with its gas spectrometer ready to measure escaping air.
questions.question: Which Mars orbit will you enter?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Dip into a low upper-atmosphere sampling orbit.
answers.consequence_summary: Sniffs atmospheric gases directly for huge science, just as a solar flare erupts!
answers.learning_point: Low periapsis orbits let spacecraft sample thin upper-atmosphere gases directly before climbing back up.

answers.text: Stay in a high, stable orbit with long Earth communication passes.
answers.consequence_summary: Protects the spacecraft from drag and delivers steady, long-term weather data.
answers.learning_point: High orbits avoid atmospheric drag, helping spacecraft last many years with minimal fuel.

questions.story: Your Mars orbiter carries wide solar wings and a heavy atmospheric dust lidar, and it needs enough rocket speed to escape Earth's gravity all the way to Mars.
questions.question: Which launch vehicle will send your orbiter to Mars?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Select a medium-class rocket meant mainly for Earth orbit.
answers.consequence_summary: The rocket lacks enough thrust to push a heavy orbiter onto a Mars transfer trajectory.
answers.learning_point: Reaching Mars requires much higher rocket speed (escape velocity) than reaching Earth orbit, reducing how much mass a rocket can carry.

answers.text: Select a heavy deep-space launch vehicle.
answers.consequence_summary: Launches cleanly to Mars, where your lidar maps global dust storms in 3D!
answers.learning_point: Deep-space missions need powerful multi-stage rockets to break free of Earth's gravity and reach another planet.

questions.story: Your ceramic heat tiles are installed! Now Flight Dynamics must plan how deeply your orbiter dips into Mars's atmosphere during aerobraking.
questions.question: How fast will you execute the aerobraking campaign?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Perform dozens of gentle, shallow passes over several weeks.
answers.consequence_summary: Keeps temperatures safe and settles smoothly into your target science orbit!
answers.learning_point: Gradual aerobraking spreads heat over many orbits, letting engineers adjust for unexpected changes in air density.

answers.text: Dive deep into thick air to finish aerobraking in three passes.
answers.consequence_summary: Unexpected air density spikes force an emergency orbit raise, cutting science time short.
answers.learning_point: Planetary atmospheres can swell unexpectedly due to dust storms or solar heating, making aggressive dives risky.

questions.story: Your nuclear-powered Mars rover and its entry aeroshell are ready for launch. Heavy interplanetary payloads require careful rocket selection.
questions.question: Which deep-space rocket configuration will you choose?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Use a proven heavy-lift interplanetary rocket.
answers.consequence_summary: Precise launch injection lands your rover in an ancient crater lakebed, discovering organic-rich clay!
answers.learning_point: Matching a spacecraft's exact mass to a proven launch vehicle maximizes mission reliability and science return.

answers.text: Pay extra for an oversized ultra-heavy rocket with huge spare capacity.
answers.consequence_summary: Reaches Mars easily, though the high launch price leaves less budget for extended rover operations.
answers.learning_point: Buying far more rocket capacity than needed drains mission budget that could fund extra science operations.

questions.story: Alert from Mars! A giant regional dust storm has darkened the sky over your solar-powered rover, dropping solar electricity to 20%.
questions.question: How will you command your rover during the dust storm?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Put the rover into low-power hibernation until winds clear the panels.
answers.consequence_summary: Protects the batteries so the rover survives, though weeks of driving time are lost.
answers.learning_point: Turning off non-essential heaters and motors during power drops helps solar rovers survive Martian dust storms.

answers.text: Keep driving and drilling at full speed during the storm.
answers.consequence_summary: Batteries drain rapidly, triggering an emergency system reset that requires replanning the mission.
answers.learning_point: When solar power drops, commanders must reduce power demand so batteries don't fall below critical levels.

questions.story: Your Mars subsurface radar has detected a huge underground ice deposit! Now you must beam the radar maps across 200 million kilometers to Earth.
questions.question: How will you manage Deep Space Network communications?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Point your 3-meter high-gain dish at NASA's Deep Space Network.
answers.consequence_summary: Giant 70-meter antennas on Earth capture your weak signal, revealing a landmark underground water map!
answers.learning_point: NASA's Deep Space Network uses giant dish antennas around Earth to hear faint radio whispers from Mars and beyond.

answers.text: Store files in onboard memory and transmit prioritized highlights.
answers.consequence_summary: Smart data prioritization sends the clearest ice-layer discoveries first without draining power.
answers.learning_point: Because Earth communication time is shared among many missions, spacecraft prioritize their most important data first.

questions.story: Space Weather Alert! The Sun just unleashed a strong solar flare, sending high-energy radiation toward Mars while your orbiter is collecting data.
questions.question: How will you respond to the solar storm?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Switch sensitive cameras to Safe Mode until radiation passes.
answers.consequence_summary: Protects electronics from radiation glitches and completes the primary mapping mission safely.
answers.learning_point: Safe Mode turns off sensitive instruments during solar storms to prevent radiation from damaging computer memory.

answers.text: Use shielded radiation sensors to record how the storm hits Mars.
answers.consequence_summary: Captures rare real-time data showing how solar storms strip gases from Mars's atmosphere!
answers.learning_point: Observing a solar storm at Mars gives scientists rare insight into how space weather affects planets without magnetic fields.

questions.story: Your low-orbit lunar mapping spacecraft passes into the Moon's dark shadow, and your small battery drops to 25% charge!
questions.question: How will you manage power until your spacecraft returns to sunlight?

source.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Space Mission Design Game

answers.text: Pause the stereo camera during shadow passes and keep only core computers on.
answers.consequence_summary: Conserves battery charge through every eclipse, completing a reliable lunar survey!
answers.learning_point: Duty-cycling—turning instruments off in shadow and back on in sunlight—lets small-battery spacecraft thrive.

answers.text: Keep heaters, transmitters, and cameras running at full power in the dark.
answers.consequence_summary: The battery runs completely flat in the shadow, shutting down the spacecraft's computers permanently.
answers.learning_point: If a spacecraft's battery drains completely in the dark, its heaters turn off and it may never wake up again.

endings.title: Outstanding Scientific Success
endings.description: Congratulations, Commander! Your spacecraft delivered groundbreaking discoveries back to Earth while balancing power, communications, and mission budget. Scientists around the world are celebrating your data!
endings.scientific_explanation: By matching your instruments, orbit, and high-gain communications to your mission objective, your spacecraft collected and transmitted complete, high-value scientific datasets.
endings.learning_point: Great space missions succeed when every subsystem—power, instruments, orbit, and communications—works together in balance.

endings.title: Successful Mission with Smart Resource Efficiency
endings.description: Mission accomplished! You designed a smart, reliable spacecraft that stayed within budget, protected its power reserves, and completed its core exploration goals.
endings.scientific_explanation: Conservative orbital choices, data compression, and smart power scheduling kept your spacecraft healthy across its entire planned lifetime.
endings.learning_point: Real space engineers often choose safe, resource-efficient designs so a mission lasts longer and delivers dependable science.

endings.title: Valuable Scientific Discovery
endings.description: Major discovery confirmed! Despite tough engineering trade-offs, your bold choices paid off with exciting new measurements that advance planetary science.
endings.scientific_explanation: Targeted instruments and careful operational margins allowed your spacecraft to gather unique data from challenging environments.
endings.learning_point: Exploring hard-to-reach places in space requires careful planning and extra safety margins, but yields extraordinary discoveries.

endings.title: Partial Mission Success
endings.description: Your spacecraft survived its journey and sent back helpful initial findings, though limited communication windows or power conservation prevented a full data return.
endings.scientific_explanation: When antenna bandwidth or solar power is constrained, spacecraft can only transmit priority summaries rather than complete high-resolution maps.
endings.learning_point: A space mission is only as productive as the data it can power and send back to Earth.

endings.title: Mission Requires a New Strategy
endings.description: Your spacecraft entered safe recovery mode after pushing environmental limits. Flight controllers have stabilized the ship, and your team is redesigning the next mission phase.
endings.scientific_explanation: Unexpected atmospheric density or dust-storm power drops forced the onboard computer to halt science operations to protect hardware.
endings.learning_point: In real spaceflight, anomalies teach engineers how to update flight software and plan safer operational margins.

endings.title: Mission Failure Due to Power or Fuel Depletion
endings.description: Contact lost! Your spacecraft ran out of battery energy or thruster propellant during a critical maneuver, ending the mission early.
endings.scientific_explanation: Without stored electrical power for heaters and radios—or propellant for attitude control—a spacecraft cannot maintain contact with Earth.
endings.learning_point: Managing power and fuel reserves is just as important as picking great cameras and sensors.

endings.title: Launch Scrubbed: Payload Mass Overload
endings.description: Hold the countdown! Pre-launch weight checks show your spacecraft is too heavy for the selected launch vehicle to reach its target trajectory.
endings.scientific_explanation: Every rocket has a strict lift-mass limit determined by its engines and propellant. Heavy payloads require heavy-lift launch vehicles.
endings.learning_point: Engineers track every kilogram during spacecraft design so the finished vehicle fits within its rocket's payload limit.

endings.title: Thermal Protection Failure During Entry
endings.description: Telemetry lost during atmospheric entry! Without proper heat shielding, friction with atmospheric gases overheated the spacecraft.
endings.scientific_explanation: Moving at kilometers per second through even a thin planetary atmosphere generates intense heat that requires specialized thermal protection.
endings.learning_point: Never sacrifice essential thermal or structural protection just to save mass—space environments are unforgiving.
